title: The code close
hook: a shared way of life for a scattered people

segments.voice: Yesterday, rehat and joy: the raag that frames the song. Your line was discipline and joy. Which routine thing did you enjoy on purpose? Day one thousand three hundred one.

A small apartment, at evening. A family stands for the Ardas, hands folded, the youngest peeking at the others to see when to bow. Half a world away, a crowded gurdwara does the same, at a different hour of the same turning planet. They have never met. They don't share a climate, a currency, or a first language for their children. But they stand at the same words, bow at the same moment in the prayer, and afterward hand out karah prashad the same way, into cupped hands. That sameness didn't happen by accident. Today we close the block on the code and look at what it built.
screen: `TWO CITIES, ONE EVENING PRAYER.` → `NEVER MET, SAME WORDS.` → `WHAT THE CODE BUILT.`

segments.voice: Walk back through this block the way you'd flip through a photo album. It opened with a plain question: who is a Sikh? Then the daily banis, rising early, the sangat and the gurdwara: how the Granth is opened and rested, what may be sung, how the hukam is taken. Readings, karah prashad, katha. No caste, no charms. Daswandh. The turban, a child's naming, the wedding and remarriage, simple funerals. Then the amrit: who gives it, what is promised, what happens when it's broken, and the penance that mends it as service. The Guru Panth, the Akal Takht and the jathedars, the Takhts one by one, the Sarbat Khalsa, the older rehatnamas, and why a code was written down at all. Then the body and the day: kesh, turbans, the kirpan and the law, kara and kangha, food, a clear mind, faithfulness at home. And last, the spirit it's kept in: love, return, children, work, your own rehat, humility and joy. Now look at what all of that adds up to. Sikhs live today in countries around the world. A people that scattered could easily have drifted into separate customs. The code gives them a shared shape instead: the same morning prayers, the same articles, the same ceremonies, the same way of serving karah prashad. And there's a line in the Ardas that holds the scattering inside it. In paraphrase: wherever the Khalsa is, there may there be protection and grace. Wherever. The prayer assumes a people spread out, and asks for them all at once. That's the block in a sentence: one way, kept in many places. And it's not the whole story. The panth also holds many orders and schools, each with its own emphasis. That's where we go next.
screen: `WHO IS A SIKH, TO HUMILITY AND JOY.` · `A SCATTERED PEOPLE, A SHARED SHAPE.` · `THE ARDAS: WHEREVER THE KHALSA IS.` · then, large: `ONE WAY, KEPT IN MANY PLACES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one practice for the panth. Choose one small thing from this block: a moment of remembrance in the morning, a clear drink, a promise kept at home, a bit of room made for a colleague, a good word instead of a score. Settle, and breathe. Picture the people around the world who keep their own version of it today, in other cities, other languages, other hours. Hold that one practice as something shared with them. If you pray, you can let Waheguru ride on the breath. The bell holds the time.
The code close. The Sikh Rehat Maryada gives a scattered people a shared way of life, and the Ardas asks for protection and grace wherever the Khalsa is. Today's word.
Your line: one way, many places. Today, keep your one practice once, and remember for a breath that someone far away is keeping theirs too. Day one thousand three hundred one.

howItsDone: Sikhs in different countries follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada as a shared reference, so the daily prayers, the five articles, the ceremonies and the serving of karah prashad look alike from one gurdwara to the next.
